newsitem.title: UK: UK rate rise not seen as blank cheque for tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: UK rate rise not seen as blank cheque for tax cuts.

text.p: The surprise decision to raise offical British interest rates by 1/4 point to six percent on Wednesday should not be viewed as a down payment for excessive tax cuts in November's budget, analysts said. Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, speaking on BBC radio after sanctioning the rate increase, denied the move would have any effect on his budget for fiscal 1997/8.
"It's got nothing to do with the budget," he said.
"The budget is there to look after public finances. I'm going to set a budget that will keep us on course for a balanced budget over the medium-term." Analysts took him at his word.
"At the margin, it shifts the odds slightly towards a looser budget, but only at the margin," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
Loynes said a fiscal giveaway, despite the political temptations raised by elections due by May 1997, would prompt Bank of England Governor Eddie George to demand tighter monetary policy still.
"This was a pre-emptive rise to get George off his back," Loynes said. George has been pressing since June for a rate rise to stem stronger growth.

Loynes said that the strength of the pound, if it is maintained, should mean no further rate increases will be needed before the elections. "Clarke probably wouldn't want to jeopardise that with a loose budget."
The pound has already gained more than six percent on a trade-weighted basis since early August and Wednesday's rate rise should give it a further boost.
An old rule of thumb is that a four percent appreciation in a nation's currency is equivalent to a one percentage point increase in interest rates, in terms of dampening inflation.

Loynes forecast tax cuts of several billion pounds in the budget, "enough to take a penny off the basic rate of tax and a few extras besides." That estimate was not swayed by Wednesday's rate rise, he said. The basic rate of income tax is 24 percent.

Britain's budget deficit, know as the Public Sector Borrowing Requirement (PSBR) certainly militates against large tax cuts. In last year's budget, Clarke forecast a PSBR of 22.5 billion pounds ($36.50 billion) in 1996/97.
That was revised up to 27.0 billion pounds in July and economists said even the second target may be breached.
Other analysts said the failure of the Conservative government to immediately follow up promises to cut taxes in the 1992 election campaign meant tax cuts may be viewed sceptically.
"A loose budget would not go down well with the electorate. Everyone knows public finances are not what they should be," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
He forecast tax cuts of around three billion pounds, offset by planned spending cuts.
On the whole, economists in the City of London, took Wednesday's credit tightening as further evidence of Clarke's credentials as a prudent finance minister.

"The Chancellor was in danger of both missing his inflation target and losing some hard won credibility," Jeremy Peat, chief economist at the Royal Bank of Scotland, said on Reuters Financial Television. "This move helps on both counts."
Clarke has a target to reduce underlying inflation to 2.5 percent. Retail prices, excluding mortgage interest payments, edged up to 2.9 percent year-on-year in September. REUTER ($1=.6165 Pound)
